title: CSS Runtime Performance
learning_outcomes: Explain css runtime performance and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply css runtime performance in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **CSS Runtime Performance** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect understanding the difference between compilation and browser rendering with reviewing selector complexity, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: Measure the part of the pipeline you want to improve. Sass affects build-time work and the CSS it emits; the browser still performs style calculation, layout, and rendering using that output.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Prefer a small, explicit output over a clever generator with many combinations. Compare CSS size and representative browser behavior before and after changes instead of treating compact source as a performance metric.

items.title: Understanding the difference between compilation and browser rendering
items.text: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact.

items.title: Reviewing selector complexity
items.text: Predict the expanded selector before compiling. Keep nesting shallow and verify that the emitted selector does not match more elements than intended.

items.title: Avoiding unnecessary DOM-wide style patterns
items.text: For avoiding unnecessary dom-wide style patterns, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

items.title: Testing layout and rendering behavior
items.text: Reproduce the issue with the smallest entrypoint, read the first relevant diagnostic, fix the source rather than the generated file, and recompile to verify the correction.

items.title: Measuring real performance rather than assuming Sass makes CSS faster
items.text: Measure the produced CSS or browser behavior and compare it against a baseline. Prefer fewer unnecessary selectors over abstractions that generate unneeded combinations.

content_blocks.expected_output: Sass preserves the modern CSS grid and min() functions; runtime behavior must be profiled in supported browsers.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Audit a small stylesheet for css runtime performance. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
